The forecasts of the experts converge on a key premise: the only realistic chance for a mutual nuclear stockpile decrease before 2026 is a new, formal bilateral agreement or extension between the United States and Russia, as China consistently and explicitly refuses to participate in any reductions. All experts note strong, public leader-level signals (Trump and Putin) supporting a one-year extension of the New START treaty, which is seen as a necessary (but not sufficient) condition for a formal agreement. However, there is debate among the experts about whether merely extending New START counts as a 'decrease,' since most proposals aim to maintain existing limits rather than reduce arsenals further.

Several positive factors are identified: synchronized elite signaling for extension (expected to slightly increase chances), strong mutual incentives to avoid an unconstrained arms race, precedent for last-minute arms control agreements, and the low threshold for question resolution (a signed agreement, not ratified, suffices).

However, all forecasts also stress sizable obstacles: a very short window remains before the deadline (less than four months), formalization of treaties usually takes substantial legal and bureaucratic effort, trust and verification are undermined by ongoing conflicts (notably Ukraine), and arms control history since the end of the Cold War shows declining base rates of new treaties. Domestic political divisions, especially in the U.S., and continued suspension of on-site inspections further decrease the likelihood.

Probability estimates vary widely due to disagreements over process risk and the technical interpretation of a New START extension: pessimistic views (7-28%) argue the extension alone may not constitute a decrease and highlight the lack of trust and time; moderate and optimistic forecasts (55-85%) emphasize (a) the technical sufficiency of an extension as a mutual agreement to cap/decrease, (b) strong elite incentives to avoid arms racing, and (c) the regularity of last-minute arms control extensions historically. Several forecasts cluster between 60-72%, citing both increased odds over historical base rates and meaningful chances for breakdown.

All agree that a trilateral agreement (including China), or a bilateral reduction involving China, is virtually impossible. The consensus is that a YES outcome is only plausible through a rapid, bilateral US-Russia extension or new reduction signed before the end of 2025, driven by high-level political will and political symbolism. A NO outcome remains plausible if delays, verification bargaining, or sudden crises stall talks or if only informal statements and not a formal signature are achieved.

In summary: Most experts see the path to YES as nontrivial but plausible due to recent diplomatic momentum and leader-level incentives, though the process remains vulnerable to breakdown. Final probabilities span from very low (7%, emphasizing the distinction between extension and true reduction) to fairly high (85%, focusing on the strong historical and institutional incentives for some formal capping agreement), with a majority clustering around 55-72% for a last-minute US-Russia agreement.
